paragraphs.title: Drink and Grain Offerings in the Land

easy.question: When will the commandments described in these verses take effect?
answers: When they are in the wilderness.
When they come to the land of their habitations.
Immediately after the giving of the Torah at Sinai.
easy.explanation: The verses clearly state: "When ye be come into the land of your habitations, which I give unto you" (verse 2).

easy.question: Which of the following animals is not mentioned as suitable for sacrifice in these verses?
answers: Calf of the herd.
Horse.
Lamb.
easy.explanation: The verses mention "of the herd or of the flock" (verse 3), which includes oxen, rams, sheep, and goats, but not horses.

easy.question: What, in addition to the animal, should be offered as part of the sacrifice?
answers: Water and fruits.
Clothes and jewelry.
A grain offering and a wine libation.
easy.explanation: The verses clearly specify to offer "a meat offering of a tenth deal of flour" (verse 4) and "wine for a drink offering" (verse 5) along with the burnt offering or sacrifice.

medium.question: What is one reason to bring an offering by fire to the Lord, as mentioned in verse 3?
answers: To give thanks for a good harvest.
To build a new altar.
In performing a vow or as a freewill offering.
medium.explanation: Verse 3 states "in performing a vow, or in a freewill offering", meaning to fulfill a vow or bring a voluntary offering.

medium.question: What does the phrase "in performing a vow" (verse 3) signify?
answers: To cancel a promise.
To fulfill a solemn promise.
To change an oath.
medium.explanation: The phrase "in performing a vow" clearly means to carry out or fulfill a solemn promise made to the Lord.

medium.question: How much fine flour is required for a grain offering for one ram?
answers: One tenth-deal.
Two tenth-deals.
Three tenth-deals.
medium.explanation: Verse 6 states: "Or for a ram, thou shalt prepare for a meat offering two tenth deals of flour".

challenge.question: What is the main principle appearing in verses 14-16 regarding the stranger?
answers: The stranger should bring lesser sacrifices than the native.
The stranger has one ordinance and one law with the native before the Lord.
The stranger is exempt from bringing sacrifices if they lack means.
challenge.explanation: Verses 15-16 clearly state: "One ordinance shall be both for you of the congregation, and also for the stranger that sojourneth with you... as ye are, so shall the stranger be before the Lord. One law and one manner shall be for you, and for the stranger that sojourneth with you", emphasizing absolute equality before the law and commandments.

challenge.question: What is the characteristic of a "sweet savour" offering to the Lord, as implied by the general biblical context and the verses?
answers: It is an offering without meat.
It is an offering intended to ward off punishment.
It is an offering desired and accepted by God.
challenge.explanation: The phrase "a sweet savour" describes an offering graciously accepted by the Lord and symbolizes man's reconciliation with God or God's grace towards him. It is not necessarily a meatless offering, nor exclusively related to warding off punishment, but rather to acceptance and favor.

challenge.question: What is the idea implied by the verse: "According to the number that ye shall prepare, so shall ye do to every one according to their number" (verse 12)?
answers: The amount of grain and drink offering is determined by the size of the animal, not the number of animals.
The drink and grain offerings must correspond to the number of animals sacrificed, with each animal having its own drink and grain offering.
It is sufficient to bring one grain and drink offering for an entire group of animals sacrificed together.
challenge.explanation: The verse emphasizes "to every one according to their number", meaning if several animals are sacrificed, each animal must have its appropriate quantities of grain and drink offering brought separately, not a single total sum for all sacrifices.

questions.question: What is the main principle appearing in verses 14-16 regarding the stranger?
answers: The stranger should bring lesser sacrifices than the native.
The stranger has one ordinance and one law with the native before the Lord.
The stranger is exempt from bringing sacrifices if they lack means.
questions.explanation: Verses 15-16 clearly state: "One ordinance shall be both for you of the congregation, and also for the stranger that sojourneth with you... as ye are, so shall the stranger be before the Lord. One law and one manner shall be for you, and for the stranger that sojourneth with you", emphasizing absolute equality before the law and commandments.

answers: It is an offering without meat.
It is an offering intended to ward off punishment.
It is an offering desired and accepted by God.
questions.explanation: The phrase "a sweet savour" describes an offering graciously accepted by the Lord and symbolizes man's reconciliation with God or God's grace towards him. It is not necessarily a meatless offering, nor exclusively related to warding off punishment, but rather to acceptance and favor.

answers: The amount of grain and drink offering is determined by the size of the animal, not the number of animals.
The drink and grain offerings must correspond to the number of animals sacrificed, with each animal having its own drink and grain offering.
It is sufficient to bring one grain and drink offering for an entire group of animals sacrificed together.
questions.explanation: The verse emphasizes "to every one according to their number", meaning if several animals are sacrificed, each animal must have its appropriate quantities of grain and drink offering brought separately, not a single total sum for all sacrifices.

easy.question: To whom is the Lord speaking in these verses?
answers: To the children of Israel directly.
To Moses, so that he may speak to the children of Israel.
To the nations dwelling in the land.
easy.explanation: Verse 17 says 'And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying', and verse 18 continues 'Speak unto the children of Israel', which indicates the message is through Moses.

easy.question: When will the children of Israel need to observe the commandment described here?
answers: Immediately upon leaving Egypt.
Only after they arrive in the land and eat of the bread of the land.
Every time they prepare bread.
easy.explanation: Verse 18 states 'When ye come into the land' and verse 19 says 'when ye eat of the bread of the land', meaning only after they settled in the land and began to use its produce.

easy.question: What type of heave offering is required from the children of Israel?
answers: An offering from any type of produce.
An offering of animals.
A cake from the first of your dough.
easy.explanation: Verse 20 explicitly says 'Ye shall offer up a cake of the first of your dough for an heave offering', meaning a specific offering from the dough.

medium.question: Why is this commandment given specifically in the context of 'When ye come into the land'?
answers: To teach them agriculture.
Because only then would they begin to eat from the produce of the promised land and not manna.
Because only in the Land of Israel can bread be made.
medium.explanation: Until their entry into the land, the children of Israel subsisted on manna in the wilderness. The commandment concerns 'the bread of the land', meaning agricultural produce of the Land of Israel, which they would only begin to eat upon entering it.

medium.question: What does the phrase "first of your dough" (verse 20) refer to?
answers: The initial quantity of seeds sown.
Dough that has been prepared for baking.
The first baked bread.
medium.explanation: "Dough" in this context refers to the mixture prepared for baking, from which a portion is separated.

medium.question: What is the significance of comparing the heave offering of dough to the "heave offering of the threshingfloor" in verse 20?
answers: That both are given at the time of harvest.
That the dough offering should only be given by farmers.
That both express the dedication of a part of the first agricultural produce to the Lord, and both have similar importance.
medium.explanation: The heave offering of the threshingfloor is a known offering from the grain after threshing. The comparison teaches that the dough offering is an equally important agricultural offering, given from the produce after it has been processed into dough, indicating its status and importance as an agricultural commandment.

challenge.question: What can be inferred from the instruction that the commandment is "in your generations" (verse 21)?
answers: That the commandment will be nullified if it is not kept.
That the commandment is temporary, only for the first generation entering the land.
That the commandment is permanently valid for all future generations of the people of Israel.
challenge.explanation: The phrase 'in your generations' in the Torah always indicates an eternal commandment or law, binding for all generations of the people of Israel, without time limit, emphasizing its permanence and importance.

challenge.question: What is the main idea expressed in the command to give the "first of your dough" to the Lord?
answers: That the Lord demands the most flawed or smallest portion.
An expression of gratitude and recognition that the Lord is the source of all abundance, and the dedication of the best and first portion to Him.
That the giving of the offering should be delayed until most of the bread has been eaten.
challenge.explanation: The giving of the 'first' (the first and best part) is a classic expression in the Torah of recognizing God as the source of blessing and owner of everything, and giving thanks for the abundance given to the people.

challenge.question: The instruction is given "When ye come into the land." What deeper meaning does this wording have beyond chronology?
answers: It hints at the need to learn new agriculture in the land.
It highlights the transition from nomadic life and the miracle of manna, to settled life and natural livelihood requiring responsibility and commitment to God for the produce of the land.
It emphasizes the difficulty of finding bread in the Land of Israel.
challenge.explanation: 'When ye come into the land' signifies not only physical entry but also a dramatic shift in lifestyle. Manna ceased upon entering the land, and the people began to cultivate the soil and live off its produce. The commandment of dough connects them to continuous gratitude for the blessing of the new land and for the Lord as their provider even in this new situation.

answers: That the commandment will be nullified if it is not kept.
That the commandment is temporary, only for the first generation entering the land.
That the commandment is permanently valid for all future generations of the people of Israel.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'in your generations' in the Torah always indicates an eternal commandment or law, binding for all generations of the people of Israel, without time limit, emphasizing its permanence and importance.

paragraphs.title: Sacrifice for Communal and Individual Unintentional Sin

easy.question: What type of sin do these verses in Numbers chapter 15, verses 22-29 discuss?
answers: Intentional sin.
Unintentional sin.
Transgression of the Ten Commandments.
easy.explanation: The verses open with the phrase "And if ye have erred" (v. 22) and emphasize "ignorance" (v. 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29) throughout, denoting a sin committed by mistake or without bad intention.

easy.question: According to the verses, who brings a sin offering when one soul sins through ignorance?
answers: The whole congregation.
The priest on behalf of the person.
The sinning person himself.
easy.explanation: Verse 27 states: "And if any soul sin through ignorance, then he shall bring a she goat of the first year for a sin offering", meaning the sinning person himself brings the sacrifice.

easy.question: What sacrifice must the congregation bring when the whole congregation sins through ignorance, in addition to the burnt offering bullock?
answers: A lamb of one year.
A she-goat of its year.
One kid of the goats for a sin offering.
easy.explanation: Verse 24 specifies: "that all the congregation shall offer one young bullock for a burnt offering... and one kid of the goats for a sin offering", meaning a kid of the goats for a sin offering.

medium.question: What does the word "ignorantly" in the phrase "the soul that sinneth ignorantly" (verse 28) mean?
answers: The rebellious soul.
The soul that sins by mistake or without intent.
The defiant soul.
medium.explanation: The word "ignorantly" (from the root ש.ג.ג) means to sin by mistake or unintentionally, as emphasized throughout these verses.

medium.question: What is the main difference in the types of sacrifices between an unintentional sin of the whole congregation and an unintentional sin of one soul?
answers: One soul brings a bullock, and the congregation brings a lamb.
One soul brings a she-goat, and the congregation brings a bullock and a kid of goats.
The sacrifices are identical, only the quantity changes.
medium.explanation: According to verse 24, the congregation brings "one young bullock for a burnt offering... and one kid of the goats for a sin offering." Whereas according to verse 27, one soul brings "a she goat of the first year for a sin offering."

medium.question: Which groups in the population receive atonement and forgiveness for unintentional sin, according to the verses?
answers: The children of Israel only.
The priests and Levites only.
The children of Israel and the strangers dwelling among them.
medium.explanation: Verse 26 explicitly states: "And it shall be forgiven all the congregation of the children of Israel, and the stranger that sojourneth among them", and verse 29 reiterates this principle: "Ye shall have one law for him that sinneth through ignorance, both for him that is born among the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them."

challenge.question: The phrase "if ought be committed by ignorance without the knowledge of the congregation" (verse 24) indicates that the sin:
answers: Was done intentionally but kept secret by the congregation.
Was known to the priests but hidden from the public.
Occurred without the awareness of the entire congregation, as a mistake or shared misunderstanding.
challenge.explanation: The phrase "without the knowledge of the congregation" implies that the entire community was unaware that it was sinning, meaning it was a collective mistake that was not perceived as a sin at the time it was committed, but was later realized to be an error.

challenge.question: What is the deeper meaning of "Ye shall have one law" (verse 29) in the context of unintentional sin, despite the differences in the details of the sacrifices?
answers: All sins, whether unintentional or intentional, can be atoned for in the same way.
The law is identical only regarding the definition of what constitutes a sin, but not regarding atonement.
The principle of atonement and forgiveness for unintentional sin applies equally to all population groups, despite differences in the details of the ritual.
challenge.explanation: "One law" emphasizes the principle of equality before the law and the Lord concerning atonement for unintentional sin, for both the native and the stranger. Although the details of the sacrifices vary, the very right to atonement and the way to achieve it is the same for all.

challenge.question: In what way do the verses emphasize the importance of the nature of the sin (unintentional versus intentional)?
answers: They specify different types of sacrifices for unintentional and intentional sins.
They present a detailed mechanism of atonement and forgiveness *only* for sins committed unintentionally.
They prescribe more severe punishments for intentional sins compared to unintentional sins.
challenge.explanation: The verses describe a specific and clear mechanism of atonement and forgiveness (bringing sacrifices by the priest) *only* for sins committed "through ignorance." The fact that there is no mention of such a way of atonement for intentional sins in the same verses emphasizes the fundamental distinction and its importance to the nature of the sin.

questions.question: The phrase "if ought be committed by ignorance without the knowledge of the congregation" (verse 24) indicates that the sin:
answers: Was done intentionally but kept secret by the congregation.
Was known to the priests but hidden from the public.
Occurred without the awareness of the entire congregation, as a mistake or shared misunderstanding.
questions.explanation: The phrase "without the knowledge of the congregation" implies that the entire community was unaware that it was sinning, meaning it was a collective mistake that was not perceived as a sin at the time it was committed, but was later realized to be an error.

questions.question: What is the deeper meaning of "Ye shall have one law" (verse 29) in the context of unintentional sin, despite the differences in the details of the sacrifices?
answers: All sins, whether unintentional or intentional, can be atoned for in the same way.
The law is identical only regarding the definition of what constitutes a sin, but not regarding atonement.
The principle of atonement and forgiveness for unintentional sin applies equally to all population groups, despite differences in the details of the ritual.
questions.explanation: "One law" emphasizes the principle of equality before the law and the Lord concerning atonement for unintentional sin, for both the native and the stranger. Although the details of the sacrifices vary, the very right to atonement and the way to achieve it is the same for all.

questions.question: In what way do the verses emphasize the importance of the nature of the sin (unintentional versus intentional)?
answers: They specify different types of sacrifices for unintentional and intentional sins.
They present a detailed mechanism of atonement and forgiveness *only* for sins committed unintentionally.
They prescribe more severe punishments for intentional sins compared to unintentional sins.
questions.explanation: The verses describe a specific and clear mechanism of atonement and forgiveness (bringing sacrifices by the priest) *only* for sins committed "through ignorance." The fact that there is no mention of such a way of atonement for intentional sins in the same verses emphasizes the fundamental distinction and its importance to the nature of the sin.

easy.question: What is the action leading to punishment in the verse?
answers: Eating forbidden food.
Acting presumptuously (defiantly).
Not bringing a sacrifice.
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly states 'But the soul that doeth ought presumptuously' (v. 30).

easy.question: Who can commit the sin mentioned in the verse?
answers: Only native-born.
Only strangers.
Both native-born and strangers.
easy.explanation: The verse says 'whether he be born in the land, or a stranger' (v. 30), meaning both a native and a stranger can commit this sin.

easy.question: What is the punishment for a person who commits this sin?
answers: He shall be cut off from among his people.
He is sent out of the land.
He must bring a special sacrifice.
easy.explanation: The verse states: 'and that soul shall be cut off from among his people' (v. 30).

medium.question: What is the central attitude described by "presumptuously" in this context?
answers: An intentional and defiant act against the Lord's commandments.
Performing a difficult task skillfully.
Giving generously to the poor.
medium.explanation: "Presumptuously" (Hebrew: `b'yad rama`) expresses an act of malice, arrogance, and intent to defy the Lord's commandments, not by mistake.

medium.question: What does the word "reproacheth" in the phrase "the same reproacheth the Lord" (verse 30) mean?
answers: He praises God.
He asks God for forgiveness.
He insults or blasphemes God.
medium.explanation: The word "reproacheth" means to scorn, insult, or blaspheme the honor of the Lord, especially in the context of defiant action.

medium.question: What is the direct consequence of "reproaching" the Lord according to the verse?
answers: The person will receive a blessing.
The person will be cut off from among his people.
The person will have to bring many sacrifices.
medium.explanation: The verse clarifies that after the person "reproacheth" the Lord, the immediate result is 'and that soul shall be cut off from among his people' (v. 30).

challenge.question: Why does the text explicitly mention both the "born in the land" (native) and a "stranger" (sojourner) in the context of this sin?
answers: To emphasize that only these two groups can commit this specific sin.
To show that the Lord's laws apply equally to all inhabitants of the land, regardless of their origin, especially in matters of severe defiance.
Because strangers were more prone to commit "presumptuous" sins.
challenge.explanation: The inclusion of the stranger alongside the native-born emphasizes the universality of the law and the demand for obedience from the entire community living in the land, granting the stranger equal status (at least concerning punishment) as part of the people.

challenge.question: What is the fundamental difference between the sin described in this verse (Numbers 15:30) and the sins requiring sin offerings mentioned earlier in the chapter (Numbers 15:22-29)?
answers: The sins in the previous verses were committed unintentionally, whereas the sin in verse 30 is intentional defiance.
The sins in the previous verses are committed by individuals, whereas the sin in verse 30 is committed by the community.
The sins in the previous verses have no consequence, whereas the sin in verse 30 has a severe consequence.
challenge.explanation: The previous verses (Numbers 15:22-29) deal with sins committed unintentionally, for which there is atonement through a sin offering. In contrast, "doeth ought presumptuously" in verse 30 refers to an intentional sin and open rebellion against the Lord, for which there is no atonement by sacrifice and the punishment is much more severe – being cut off.

challenge.question: The phrase "and that soul shall be cut off from among his people" (verse 30) implies what about the nature of this punishment in ancient Israelite society?
answers: This was a temporary exile from the community.
It referred to the loss of property and social status, but with physical remaining in the community.
It signified a complete spiritual and often physical separation, similar to excommunication or even premature death, severing ties with the covenant community.
challenge.explanation: The punishment of 'karet' (being cut off) is one of the most severe punishments in the Torah, indicating a complete severance from the people and the covenant with the Lord, both in life and in the afterlife. It is more significant than merely physical expulsion, and is often interpreted as premature death or barrenness.

paragraphs.title: The Man Gathering Sticks on the Sabbath

easy.question: What did the children of Israel find in the wilderness on the Sabbath day?
answers: A man gathering sticks.
A well of water.
A bag of food.
easy.explanation: The first verse (32) explicitly states: "And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day".

easy.question: To whom was the man found gathering sticks brought?
answers: Only to the princes of the people.
To Moses, Aaron, and all the congregation.
To the High Priest in the Temple.
easy.explanation: Verse 33 states: "And they that found him gathering sticks brought him unto Moses and Aaron, and unto all the congregation".

easy.question: What was the man's final sentence?
answers: A heavy monetary fine.
Exile from the camp.
Death by stoning.
easy.explanation: Verse 35 states: "And the Lord said unto Moses, The man shall be surely put to death: all the congregation shall stone him with stones without the camp".

medium.question: Why was the man kept "in ward", as described in verse 34?
answers: To give him time to reflect on his actions.
Because it was not yet determined what his punishment would be.
Because there was a fear he might escape from the camp.
medium.explanation: The verse clarifies: "And they put him in ward, because it was not declared what should be done to him", meaning it was not yet known what judgment should be imposed on him.

medium.question: What does the word "declared" in the phrase "it was not declared what should be done to him" (verse 34) mean?
answers: Revealed.
Made clear/specified.
Forgiven.
medium.explanation: The word "declared" (from the root פ.ר.ש) means clarified, specified, or explained. In the context of the verse, "it was not declared what should be done to him" means that the punishment was not yet clear or defined.

medium.question: What is the correct order of events from the moment the man was found until his death?
answers: Finding the man, his death, bringing him to Moses, the command from the Lord.
Finding the man, bringing him to Moses, putting him in ward, the command from the Lord, execution.
Bringing him to Moses, the command from the Lord, finding the man, execution.
medium.explanation: The chronological order in the verses is: finding the man (verse 32), bringing him to Moses and Aaron (verse 33), putting him in ward (verse 34), the Lord's command (verse 35), and execution (verse 36).

challenge.question: What is the meaning of the command "all the congregation shall stone him with stones without the camp" (verse 35) regarding the community's responsibility?
answers: This was to ensure that no single individual had direct responsibility for the death.
The command emphasizes the importance of passive involvement of the entire congregation in the punishment.
It places collective responsibility on the entire community for enforcing the law and emphasizes the severity of the offense.
challenge.explanation: The involvement of "all the congregation" (the entire community) in carrying out the punishment emphasizes the severity of the offense as a harm to the entire community, and the shared responsibility of all to uphold the laws and remove evil from their midst. It is a public act that strengthens the authority of the law.

challenge.question: What might be the reason for carrying out the punishment "without the camp" (verse 35)?
answers: To prevent people inside the camp from witnessing the act.
To symbolize that the offender was expelled from the holy community and declared outside the sacred boundaries of the camp.
So that the punishment would be carried out in a remote place and be easier to perform.
challenge.explanation: Expulsion from the camp in cases of severe offenses (as well as for the unclean) was meant to symbolize the removal of impurity and evil from within the holiness of the camp, the place where the Lord dwells. The offender is cast out beyond the boundaries of the holy community.

challenge.question: What can be learned from this passage about the status of Sabbath observance during the period of the children of Israel in the wilderness?
answers: Sabbath observance was important, but its violation did not necessarily lead to severe punishment.
Violation of the Sabbath was considered a particularly severe offense, punishable by death, and this indicates its centrality in the system of laws and faith.
It was a relatively new law, which the people had not yet internalized its severity, and therefore an example needed to be set.
challenge.explanation: The fact that a person was punished with a severe death penalty (stoning) for forbidden work on the Sabbath, after direct consultation with the Lord, shows that Sabbath observance was considered a most fundamental and severe commandment, and that its violation was a deep offense to the divine and social order of the people.

answers: This was to ensure that no single individual had direct responsibility for the death.
The command emphasizes the importance of passive involvement of the entire congregation in the punishment.
It places collective responsibility on the entire community for enforcing the law and emphasizes the severity of the offense.
questions.explanation: The involvement of "all the congregation" (the entire community) in carrying out the punishment emphasizes the severity of the offense as a harm to the entire community, and the shared responsibility of all to uphold the laws and remove evil from their midst. It is a public act that strengthens the authority of the law.

answers: To prevent people inside the camp from witnessing the act.
To symbolize that the offender was expelled from the holy community and declared outside the sacred boundaries of the camp.
So that the punishment would be carried out in a remote place and be easier to perform.
questions.explanation: Expulsion from the camp in cases of severe offenses (as well as for the unclean) was meant to symbolize the removal of impurity and evil from within the holiness of the camp, the place where the Lord dwells. The offender is cast out beyond the boundaries of the holy community.

answers: Sabbath observance was important, but its violation did not necessarily lead to severe punishment.

paragraphs.title: The Commandment of Fringes (Tzitzit) and its Meaning

easy.question: What is the main commandment that God commands the children of Israel in these verses?
answers: To make fringes on the borders of their garments.
To offer sacrifices.
To build a tabernacle.
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly states: "and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations".
